hire_for: Turn vague product claims into specific, checkable facts and test offers small, judged by what each customer cost you.
store_questions: Read my product page as a salesman at the door: which words like 'premium' or 'best' should go, and what plain fact with a number replaces each?
What do we do in making this product that rivals also do but never mention, and how would you turn it into the reason to buy?
Write 10 headlines for my best seller, each aimed at a different kind of buyer, so I can test the top few against each other.
Design a sample or trial offer that only reaches people who read our story and asked for it, with a code so I can track each one.
Before I spend my launch budget, split it into a small test with a tracked link per ad and a cost per customer I must hit to scale.
Am I trying to change a habit with this product, and is each new buyer worth what it costs me to convert them?

hire_for: Find the desire your buyers already have, then match the headline to how aware they are and how many claims they have heard.
store_questions: Here are 30 reviews and my product facts: what strong want do buyers already have that this product meets, in their own words?
How aware is my buyer of the problem and of my brand, and what should the first line of my ad say at that level?
Every brand in my category makes the same claim. How many times have buyers heard it, and what would be new to them?
My sales page leads with features. Rebuild the order so the want comes first and each claim is set up before it is made.
Which claim on my page will buyers not believe at the top, and what has to come before it?
Give me two very different versions of my landing page to test, not near twins, and say what each one bets on.

hire_for: Build product pages and ads on research and real facts, with one big idea that sells and a steady brand voice.
store_questions: Review my best ad and tell me plainly whether it will sell, and why, as a busy shopper reading it once would see it.
Write 20 headlines for my product page from real product facts, then pick the three I should test first.
Describe my brand as a person in one paragraph, then mark which of my current ads chip away at that personality.
Should I run another 20 percent off sale or put the money into ads that build the brand? Show me the trade-off.
Does my video ad still tell the story with the sound off? List what to change so it does.
Write a short sales guide for my support team: how to open, what to stress and how to answer the top three objections.

hire_for: Make sales emails and pages sound like one person talking, with a promise buyers can picture, a bold guarantee and a clear ask.
store_questions: Rewrite my launch email so it sounds like me writing to one friend, not a company, and asks clearly for the order.
What exactly is the promise on my product page, and could a buyer picture the result? Make it concrete.
Write a simple, bold guarantee for my best seller that I would be glad to honour, and show me where it goes on the page.
Which proven ads and emails in my category should I study and copy out by hand, and what makes each one work?
Tear my sales page apart the way a tough hot-seat group would, and mark every place a reader would stop reading.

hire_for: Write long product pages people finish: a true story up top, the honest drawback said first, easy ordering and a small test first.
store_questions: Here is how I found this product. Turn the true story into an opening for my product page that makes buyers read the next line.
Read my product page and show me where the reader stops sliding down the page, and why.
What is the honest drawback of my product, and how would you say it first so it builds trust?
Plan a simple demo video with real people trying my product, for my product page and my ads.
How many steps does it take to order on my store right now, and which ones would you cut?
What backend offer should follow the first sale: an add-on, a bundle or a refill plan?

hire_for: Write headlines and subject lines that say what the reader gets, then compare two versions fairly with tracked results.
store_questions: Write 20 headlines for my offer, sorted into self-interest, news and curiosity, ready to test.
Cover everything but the headline on my homepage: would a stranger know what they get? Rewrite it so they would.
My ad gets clicks but few sales. Work out why it gets seen but not answered.
Which one appeal should my product lead with: save money, look good or feel safe? Say why.
Plan a fair test of two email subject lines: one difference, matched halves of my list, and how to tell a real win from luck.
Here are my last test results. What should I keep, drop and test next?

hire_for: Write cart, follow-up and win-back emails that start where the buyer's thoughts already are and add a new reason each time.
store_questions: Rewrite my abandoned cart email so the first line talks about what the shopper wants, not about us or the price.
Write three openings for the same offer, each aimed at a different kind of buyer on my list.
My first email gets opened but not answered. Plan a short follow-up series where each email adds a new reason to buy.
Turn the feature list for my best seller into a word picture the buyer can see themselves in.
What bait would my lapsed customers bite on, and how does my offer move them a step closer to what they want?
Write a polite reminder for a subscriber whose payment failed that keeps their goodwill.

hire_for: Plan long sales pages around the buyer's strongest feeling, with proof beside every claim and each yes the buyer must give mapped.
store_questions: What keeps my buyer awake at night about this problem, and where on my landing page do we touch it?
Outline my sales page from headline to P.S. before any copy, showing what each section must sell before the next starts.
List every claim on my page and the proof a doubter would need for each. Mark the ones I can't prove yet.
Turn my flat feature list into benefits, then give me the benefit of each benefit, two levels deep.
Check my page against the eight yeses a buyer must give before they buy, and show me where it loses them.
Turn these plain customer quotes into a headline and a short story for my page.

hire_for: Put a clear offer, a true reason to act now and tracking into every ad and email, then follow up the almost-buyers.
store_questions: Where is the offer in my ad, why would someone act today and not next month, and what exactly do I tell them to do?
Add a real reason to buy now to my promotion, like a true deadline or limited stock, with nothing fake.
Set up simple tracking so I know which ad, email or post brought each customer.
What happens to people who added to cart and left? Plan who contacts them next, with what, and when.
Which of my marketing costs can't show a result, and which should I cut first?
Who exactly is my product for? Narrow my market and match the message and the channel to it.

hire_for: Write a sharp brief, fix the offer before the words and plan what happens after the first email gets no reply.
store_questions: Here is my brief for a new email campaign. What exactly am I saying, to whom, and what is missing?
Why do my best customers really buy, and could a small change to what I sell make a better offer?
Is there a person in my emails, or just a brochure? Who should be speaking, and why would buyers believe them?
Run my next promotion through a direct marketing checklist before it goes out, and list what it misses.
My first email got no reply. Plan the next three messages as a campaign, not a one-off.
I'm choosing an agency or freelancer. What should I ask, and how will I count what their work brings in?

hire_for: Back every claim with proof a sceptic would accept, and build a believable offer with a reason for the deal and a strong guarantee.
store_questions: Read my landing page as a 'yeah, sure' sceptic and set the proof I have beside every claim. Which claims should go?
Audit what I run now: headline, body, bullets, offer, guarantee and free gift. Which part could a challenger beat?
What am I really selling? What else could my product be to the buyer?
Give me why us, why it's true and why now for my best seller.
Build my offer: one thing per ad, a believable reason for the deal, a deluxe option and an honest limit.
Where is the hungry crowd already looking for this, and how can we prove it small before we bet big?

hire_for: Find one honest idea for your brand and say it in a fresh way, even turning a weakness into the reason to buy.
store_questions: What's the idea behind my brand? Not the facts, the idea. Would anyone notice my ads among all the others in their feed?
What's the weakness I'm hiding about my product, and could it become the reason to buy?
If a rival said the plain version of my tagline, could anyone tell us apart? Rewrite it so they could.
Does the picture in my ad make the same point as the words? Show me where they split.
Ask me for the facts first, then give me three fresh ways to say the one thing my product does better.

hire_for: Write product copy from the life of the person who really decides to buy, with a useful how-to that sells.
store_questions: Who actually decides to buy my product, and is anyone like them shaping my copy?
Rewrite my product description around what it does for my buyer's day, not just how it looks on the shelf.
Write a short numbered routine buyers could try tonight with my product, so my how-to guide sells.
Would my buyer believe this line, or roll their eyes? Mark the promises my product can't keep.
Should I use famous or ordinary customers in my testimonials, and who does my buyer trust on this?

hire_for: Write warm, one-breath taglines for personal products buyers feel shy about, and answer their private fears in plain words.
store_questions: What private question is my buyer asking about this product, and can it become my headline?
My product carries a little stigma. How do I promise discretion, not display, in my ads?
Write five taglines a buyer could say to a friend in one breath.
What is my buyer afraid will go wrong, and have my product page and ads answered it plainly?
Who does my buyer already trust on this, like a hairdresser or a pharmacist, and how can my ads borrow that trust honestly?
Can my campaign idea run for years with new lines? Give me the next five.

hire_for: Find the sizzle and the first ten words that sell, and turn yes-or-no questions into which-one choices in chat and on the page.
store_questions: What's the sizzle in my product: what will buyers see, hear, smell or picture? Rewrite my first ten words around it.
My chat replies ask 'Do you want it?' Rewrite them to ask 'Which one?' and win a small yes first.
Give me a ten-second opening line for my live chat, two spares, and the signals that a shopper is ready to buy.
How can shoppers hold, try or see my product work, on the page or in a video?
Is this objection honest, a test or a stall? Give me a reply for each of my top three.
Write three versions of my add-to-cart nudge to test, and tell me how to keep the winner.

hire_for: Rewrite landing pages and emails from mined customer words, cut claims that fail 'so what, prove it', then test against the control.
store_questions: Mine these reviews by hand: mark the phrases that repeat and surprise, and turn the best into headlines for my landing page.
Run every claim on my homepage through 'so what, prove it' and tell me what to cut or back up.
Is the shopper ready for my Add to cart button yet? Build the page backward from the button.
Lay out my product page as Problem, Promise, Proof, Proposal, using my research to fill each part.
Audit my welcome email flow as the control before you rewrite it: what works, what to protect and what to fix?
If my next test loses, what will we have learned? Write the hypothesis before the copy.

hire_for: Grow sales through all three levers, more buyers, bigger orders and more repeat buying, using assets the store already owns.
store_questions: What am I sitting on that I don't use: past buyers, my email list, a partner brand with the same customers?
Split my growth into more buyers, bigger orders and more repeat buying. What would a 10 percent gain on each add up to?
What is a customer worth to me over time, by source, and how much can I afford to pay to win one?
Who carries the risk in my offer right now? Write a guarantee or trial that moves it to me.
Plan a referral system my happiest customers would actually use.
Which other brand already sells to my buyers, and what joint offer could we make together?

hire_for: Build an offer buyers can't compare to rivals: list every worry, stack the fixes, price from the worth and keep scarcity honest.
store_questions: If a buyer put my product next to a rival's, what would they compare? Make my offer one they can't compare.
List every worry between my buyer and the result they want, then turn each into a bonus, a fix or a guarantee.
Score my offer on dream outcome, likelihood, time and effort, then fix the weakest part and make the fix visible.
I want to raise prices. What is my product worth to buyers, and what is my price as a share of that?
Add a real cap, a real date and a guarantee with the refund sums done. If refunds doubled but sales rose a third, am I better off?
Is my market starving for this and able to pay, or is the market the problem and not the offer?

hire_for: Map the path from first visit to repeat order: a hook, story and offer, then a value ladder with a subscription rung.
store_questions: What's the next step after someone lands on my store? Map my funnel from first visit to repeat order.
Build a value ladder for my store: an entry product, the core product, an upsell and a subscription or refill.
What's the hook, story and offer for my best seller's ad? Would the hook stop someone scrolling?
Tell my founder story so buyers reach the same insight I did, and cut it to fit a product page.
My product isn't selling. Before I blame the product, what in the pitch should I test first?
Which one funnel actually drives my growth, and which others should feed it or stop?

hire_for: Grow by reaching more light buyers and being easy to notice and buy, judged on buying data, not surveys or loyalty myths.
store_questions: Should I start a loyalty program, or put the money into reaching more new buyers? Use my order data, not a survey.
How many of my buyers are light buyers who buy once a year, and are my ads reaching people like them at all?
In which buying moments does my brand come to mind, and in which does it vanish?
How easy is it to find and buy my product right now, on my store, on marketplaces and in search?
Which of my brand assets, like colour, logo, pack or sound, are distinctive enough to use in every ad?
This vendor says their tool has no wasted spend. Who sells this metric, and what would they lose if it didn't matter?

hire_for: Split ad budget between brand building and sales ads, compare share of voice with share of market, and check sales were really extra.
store_questions: I spend almost everything on retargeting and Shopping ads. How should I split my budget between brand and sales, starting near 60:40?
What's my share of voice compared with my share of market, and am I underspending?
Would these sales have happened without the ad? How do I check before I cut or scale?
Is each of my ads built to build the brand or to trigger a sale, and is it emotional or clear enough for that job?
Growth has slowed. Should I cut spend? What does the long-run data say beyond this quarter?
How should I combine a holdout test, modelling and platform attribution to judge my ads?

hire_for: Write the marketing plan in the right order: diagnose, pick the target, set the position and goals, and only then choose tactics.
store_questions: Here is my marketing plan. Is it a strategy or a list of channels? Rebuild it as diagnosis, target, position and objectives.
Who exactly is my target buyer, and who am I leaving out on purpose?
Write my position in one sentence a customer would recognise.
What am I doing for the 95 percent of my market who aren't ready to buy yet?
Would a viewer name my brand a day after seeing my ad? Which four or five distinctive assets should I use boldly?
Everyone says I should be on this new platform. Where's the evidence, and why not do both?

hire_for: Pick the one word your brand can own in buyers' minds, decide what to give up, and stop stretching one name over everything.
store_questions: First what? What kind of product could my brand be the first of in buyers' minds?
What one word could my brand own, and does a rival already hold it?
Should I add these new products under my brand name, or would a new name serve them better?
What should I give up, in products or buyers, to make my position clearer?
I'm launching a brand nobody knows. What would a reporter write about it, and how do I get that story first?
My category is splitting. Should I lead the new branch, and what name would carry it?

hire_for: Size up the category leader, find the weakness inside its strength and claim a different idea you can prove.
store_questions: Who leads my category, and what do they own in buyers' minds?
Where is the leader weak because of its strength, the thing it can't fix because of what it is?
What are my credentials for the idea I want to own? Show me which proof I have and which I lack.
Does my ad say something different, or just something nice? Rewrite my slogan to set me apart.
Brief my designer with the idea settled first: the words, then the pictures that back them.
My position feels tired. How do I reposition against rivals without a head-on fight with the leader?

hire_for: Change how the store feels before changing what it costs: reframe the brief, find what each step signals and test the odd idea.
store_questions: Delivery takes five days and I can't make it faster. What would make the wait feel better, even if it works exactly the same?
What do my packaging, price and free returns signal to a first-time buyer, and what would it cost a rival to fake them?
I want to cut handwritten thank-you notes and live chat to save money. What do they do that nobody wrote down?
What is the opposite of the obvious idea for more repeat orders, and could I test the silly version cheaply this week?
Which part of my buying journey should be slower, not faster, to make the product feel worth more?
Am I answering the question in my brief, or the one my shoppers actually have?

hire_for: Use true social proof, real scarcity, authority and giving first on product pages and offers, with an ethics check on each.
store_questions: Which persuasion principle is really at work on my product page, and which one is missing?
What could I give buyers first that feels personal and unexpected, not a generic gift with strings?
How should I show what people like my buyer already do, using true numbers from my orders and reviews?
What is truly unique about my offer, and what do buyers lose by passing? Cut any scarcity that isn't real.
What will shoppers have just seen right before they reach my price, and how should I change it?
Am I stacking every principle on one page? Tell me which to keep and which to drop.

hire_for: Check forecasts, price framing and test results for bias: take the outside view and agree in advance what would prove you wrong.
store_questions: Here is my sales forecast for the holiday season. How did similar launches turn out, and what range should I plan for?
Would my buyers choose differently if my price or offer were framed as a loss instead of a gain?
My last A/B test won big on a small sample. Is it settled, and what would I expect to see if I were wrong?
What's missing from the story I'm telling myself about why sales dropped last month?
Break my decision to launch a new product line into parts, so each partner scores them alone before we talk.
Which moments of delivery and unboxing will buyers remember most, and are those moments good?

hire_for: Position your product against the alternatives buyers really consider, and turn unique features into value the right buyers want.
store_questions: Compared with what? List what my buyers would use if my product didn't exist, counting only what shows up on real shortlists.
Map what my product does that those alternatives can't, then ask 'so what' until each has a value a buyer would choose me for.
Which of my selling points are real value, and which are just objection handlers like free returns or a badge?
Who cares most about my value? Study why I win sales, not why I lose them.
Which market frame makes my value easiest to see: what category should my homepage say I'm in?
A bigger rival says they do what I do. How should my product page answer that?

hire_for: Sharpen what makes your brand different with the onliness test and a rival grid, so buyers get a clear gut feeling about you.
store_questions: Who are we, what do we do, and why does it matter? Give me a sharp answer for my store.
Finish 'We are the only...' for my brand, then swap in a rival's name. Does it still fit?
Map my rivals the way customers see them, on a grid of the factors that matter. Where is the white space?
Is this new product line making my brand sharper or blurrier?
What do customers say about my brand when I'm not in the room? Use these reviews.
How could I test a risky new idea small, perhaps under a separate name, so the main brand is safe if it fails?

hire_for: Make ads people would choose to watch, built on distinctive assets that tie the entertainment back to your brand.
store_questions: Would anyone choose to watch my ad? Am I entertaining people in their feed, or boring them?
What will people remember that ties my ad to my brand: a character, a tune, a look or a name?
My brand has no big budget. Where's the showman in my plan, and what would get people talking?
My brief asks for one rational point. Is that really the job?
If a rival copied my logo tomorrow, what else would still say it's us?

hire_for: Make your product talkable with triggers, visible use and stories, and remove the barriers that stop buyers switching to you.
store_questions: Why would someone talk about my product? What does sharing it say about them?
What in my buyer's daily life could remind them of my product, and how do I tie my posts to it?
How can I make people using my product visible to others, the way a laptop logo faces onlookers?
Shoppers like my product but stay with what they use now. What is stopping them, before I push harder?
How can I make my product easier and less risky to try: a sample, a trial or a free swap?
Score my content plan on social currency, triggers, emotion, public, practical value and stories.

hire_for: Make your homepage clear in eight seconds: the buyer as hero, your brand as guide, a three-step plan and a plain buy button.
store_questions: Can a stranger tell what I sell, how it helps and how to buy within eight seconds on my homepage?
What does my customer want, in one sentence, and what problem stands in the way on all three levels?
Who is the hero of my product page, me or the buyer? Rewrite it with my brand as the guide.
Give me a three-step plan that shows how buying from me works.
Write a one-liner for my store that someone in a coffee queue could repeat.
What happens if my buyer doesn't act, and what does life look like if they do?

hire_for: Pick the smallest audience your store can delight, earn permission to email them and make the product worth talking about.
store_questions: Who is my store for, exactly? Name the smallest group I could serve well enough to keep the shop going.
Did my subscribers ask to hear from me? Would they complain if my emails stopped?
Is my product itself worth talking about, or am I using stunts to draw eyes to something ordinary?
Would anyone miss my brand if it were gone? What change am I trying to make for my buyers?
Sales are slow. Is this a dip worth pushing through, or a dead end I should quit?
How can I help my customers connect with each other, so they feel 'people like us buy this'?

hire_for: Make your message stick with one core idea and a concrete example, and design peak moments into unboxing and first use.
store_questions: What is the core of my brand message, in one sentence a new customer would get?
Which words on my site only make sense to me? Find the curse of knowledge and make them concrete.
Where is the peak in my customer's journey, and how can I build one into unboxing or first use?
What do shoppers expect from my category, and where can I break that script?
I keep going round on whether to launch this product. Give me two more options besides yes or no, and a tripwire.
Turn a number from my business, like bottles saved or orders shipped, into a picture a buyer can see.

hire_for: Work backwards from the customer: write the launch press release first, set goals on inputs you control and move fast on reversible calls.
store_questions: Before I build this new product, write the press release and the hard customer questions. Would a buyer care?
What need of my buyers will still be true in ten years, and am I investing in it: price, range or fast delivery?
Is my decision to switch shipping partners a door I can walk back through? How fast should I decide?
I watch ROAS every day. Which input goals I control, like range, in-stock rate or delivery speed, should I set instead?
Am I copying a rival's move, or building something my customers asked for in their own words?
What does this bet cost if it fails and pay if it works, and can my store survive the miss?

hire_for: Cut waste so you can charge less, walk rivals' stores with a notepad and ask your front-line team what customers really say.
store_questions: Go through my costs line by line: which ones could I do cheaper so I can charge customers less?
Walk my top three rivals' stores with a notepad: what do they do better than me, and what should I copy?
My support team talks to customers every day. What should I ask them this week, and how do I get them talking?
Everyone in my niche is going one way. What's the other way?
How should I keep score with my small team, with a friendly contest and a promise if we hit the number?
A customer got a bad order. How do I make it right fast, with no excuses?

hire_for: Design products and the range to a price your buyers can afford, cut cost without cutting the quality they need, and keep the range tight.
store_questions: Who is my product for, and can they afford it? Set the target price first, then design the product to hit it.
Where can I lower the cost of my best seller through design, buying, shipping or materials, without cutting the quality buyers need?
Could I get the same result from my launch with half the money? Show me how.
My range has grown to 200 products. Am I spreading myself too thin, and what should I cut?
Why do we do it this way? Question three habits in my fulfilment that nobody has checked.

hire_for: Test a product idea cheaply with your own money, then win the first big buyer and the shop floor by showing the product in person.
store_questions: Is this a problem I have myself, and who else has it? How do I ask them before I spend?
What's the cheapest way to test my product idea this month with my own money, while I keep my day job?
What can I do myself, like a first patent draft or my listings, and what should I pay an expert for?
Who is the one buyer or stockist who could change everything, and how do I show them the product in person?
Is my product ten times better than what's out there, or just a bit better? Be honest.
Where will my customer actually see my product, and how do I win over the staff who sell it there?

hire_for: Keep the store simple for buyers and your team: one hard-to-fake number, fast reversible calls and tools before new hires.
store_questions: Does this new app or feature make my store simpler for the shopper, or just busier?
What one number should my store steer by that is hard to fake, and how do I review it each week?
How undoable is this decision to change my store platform or theme? Should I try it now or slow down?
Before I hire someone new, could AI or a better tool do the work first?
Which of my processes make something possible, which make it simpler, and which should go?
Will this change create long-term value for my customers, even if it costs revenue now?

hire_for: Make service the brand: values you can hire by, support that puts the experience before speed, and ad money moved into service.
store_questions: Write three core values for my store that I could really hire and fire by.
My support team rushes customers to cut handle time. Should we aim for the best experience instead, and what does it cost?
What would make a customer tell their friends about my support?
What is the opposite of what every store in my niche does for service?
Should I move some ad budget into service, like free returns or faster replies? Show me the trade-off.
How do I check a new support hire for culture fit as well as skills?

hire_for: Build products that last, offer repair, find and stop your biggest harm, and grow at a pace you can pay for yourself.
store_questions: Should I launch a cheaper version of my product to win sales? What would it do to the brand?
What is the most harm my products do, and how do I stop it, step by step down my supply chain?
Is my product the best I can make? Will it last, and could I offer repair?
Do I need to grow this fast, or do I just want to? Can I pay for this growth from my own earnings?
Would a buyer purchase this if they already owned one that worked? How do I sell to that?
Which green claims on my site cover a harm instead of fixing it?

hire_for: Launch with samples and demonstrations instead of ad money, pick stockists that make the brand look better and train who sells it.
store_questions: I have no ad budget. Where is my buyer a captive audience with time to try my product, and how do I put samples there?
What will a first-time buyer take home today: a sample, a gift with purchase or a mini?
Does this discount make my brand look better or cheaper?
Is this stockist, marketplace or pop-up the right place for my brand, and what does it say about us?
How do I show a big stockist there is demand before I ask for the order?
Write a first-minute script for whoever sells my product, in store or on live video.

hire_for: Build trust strangers can rely on into your offer, win where you know the ground better than big rivals, and grow with small partners.
store_questions: Why would a stranger trust my store with their money? What can I build into checkout to hold that trust, like a guarantee or a delivery promise?
Where do I know the ground better than the big marketplaces and rivals? Where is my river?
Who else grows if my store grows: suppliers, creators or small stockists? How do I build that?
Does my plan pass the ten-year test, or does it only pay this year?
What do I have, what do I want, and what will I give up to get there?
Could my store run for a month without me? What has to change first?

hire_for: Turn what your brand stands for into practical action buyers can see: refills, checked suppliers and a cause in your shop window.
store_questions: What does my brand stand for, and could a customer see it on my store today?
Who made my products and what were they paid? How do I check my suppliers myself instead of trusting a promise?
What waste can I cut tomorrow: refills, reused boxes or plainer packaging?
Should my brand take a stand on this issue? Is it brave enough, or only nice, and what might it cost in sales?
What would I put on my homepage if it wasn't a product?
Am I training my support team to sell, or to know the products deeply?

hire_for: Sell by showing and teaching how the product works, and build a trained team of sellers or ambassadors who earn well.
store_questions: Who has the same problem I had, and how do I show them the product working in their own hands?
Turn my product page into a lesson that teaches care and use, not just a list of what's in the jar.
Plan an ambassador program where I train customers to sell, and make sure they earn properly.
What can I start with today, using only what I have, to get the first sales from friends and neighbours?
How should I run prizes for my ambassadors: for sales, for recruiting and for giving back locally?

hire_for: Create a new category instead of fighting in a crowded one, own the events where buyers are and hold a premium price as the original.
store_questions: Is there a market for my product yet, or do I have to create one? What would I name the new category?
Testers disliked my product's name and taste. How should I read bad test results like that?
Where are my buyers in real life, like events, sports or campuses, and how do I become part of that world, not just a logo on it?
Should I sponsor this event, or create a small event of my own?
Copycats are undercutting me. How do I hold my premium price as the original?

hire_for: Make each product more desirable: sort the range into stars, rising stars and ones to sell, and guard rarity and quality.
store_questions: Does this new product make my brand more desirable, or just bigger?
Sort my range into stars, rising stars and products I should drop, and say where the money should go.
Should I launch a cheaper line? What would it do to desire for the main range?
Which part of my brand is timeless and which part is modern? Is the balance right?
Is my quality beyond question down to the smallest detail, like stitching, packaging and the first email?

hire_for: Design a fashion range around a few signature details, simple lines and real use, and judge each trend as style or passing fashion.
store_questions: Can my customers move, sit and work in this piece? What should come off it?
What is the one detail that makes my products mine? Would people know they're ours without the label?
Customers are asking for this season's trend. Is it style or just fashion, and should I make it?
What humble material, or idea from sport or menswear, could make my next product better?
Pick three signatures for my brand and show me how to repeat them across the range.
Should I license my brand name to a partner, and who would control what's made under it?

hire_for: Find the next product by watching how buyers really use things, launch a few items, and plan a line that renews each year.
store_questions: What do my customers do with my product when nobody tells them how? Plan how I watch and ask.
What is on the shelf in my category that buyers don't really want, and what is clearly missing?
Turn my one hit into a line: which few items do I launch, and what new ones each year?
A big retailer said no to my product. Who else can I ask, and can I reach buyers directly?
How much can I lose on this big marketing bet and still be standing?
What does my product let buyers dream about, and does that frame hold up when I ask them?

hire_for: Walk the store as a customer, add up the small shortcuts that took the feel out of it, and get back to the core as you grow.
store_questions: Walk through my store as a first-time customer: what do you see and feel from the homepage to the delivery box?
List the small shortcuts I've taken, like cheaper packaging or canned emails, and what they add up to.
What was my store for on day one, and am I still doing it?
What would make my store a place people come back to, not just buy from once?
Am I opening new product lines because it's right, or because I can? Which should I close?
Would my team say this is a company that looks after them?

hire_for: Take on the big, lazy player in your niche, launch with a story the press will cover and cap the downside before a bold bet.
store_questions: Who's the big, lazy player in my niche, and what annoys their customers that I could fix?
Is my product truly different, more fun, more human or better value, or is it a copy with no reason to switch?
How could my launch make the news without paid ads? Give me three story angles.
What's the worst case on this bold bet, and how do I cap it, like a right to hand back stock?
Would this new product line strengthen my brand name or hurt it?
What do my front-line support people think of this idea, and how do I ask them?

hire_for: Prove a product idea with real pre-sales in a weekend: one-minute maths, ten people to ask and a pay button, not a survey.
store_questions: Do the one-minute maths on my product idea: price, profit per sale and how many sales hit my goal.
Plan my weekend pre-sale: ten people to ask, what to say, and how I take money before I order stock.
Who has paid me so far? Is my waitlist proof, or just interest?
Nobody paid in my pre-sale. What do I change: the offer, the price or the buyer?
Score my marketing ideas 1 to 5 on impact and ease, and tell me which to stop.
When someone says no, how do I ask for a referral or offer a smaller deal?

hire_for: Strip a product, pack or page down to what earns its place, honest and built to last, using his ten design checks.
store_questions: What is my product for, in one sentence, and which parts or features don't serve that purpose?
If I had to remove one thing from my packaging, what would it be?
Does my product explain itself without a manual? Where would a buyer get stuck?
Review my new product design against the ten principles and list what fails.
Will this product still be right in ten years? What does it cost to make, use and throw away?
Is any part of my product page or pack there to impress rather than to help?

hire_for: Find why shoppers fail at checkout and forms: blame the design, not the user, and fix the cues, feedback and error recovery.
store_questions: Shoppers keep failing at my checkout. Walk through it step by step and show me where the design leads them wrong.
On my product page, what tells a shopper what to do next? Where are the cues missing?
After a shopper taps Add to cart, how do they know it worked? Is my feedback clear?
When a shopper makes a mistake, like a wrong size or a bad address, how easily can they recover?
What does a shopper think my size picker or bundle builder does, and does it match how it works?
Plan how I watch three real people try to buy from my store, and what to note.

hire_for: Run a cheap monthly test where your team watches three shoppers use the store, then fix the worst problems with the smallest change.
store_questions: If a stranger saw my homepage for five seconds, what would they think it is? What should change?
Write the script and three tasks for a monthly test where I watch three shoppers use my store.
Which choice on my product page makes a shopper hesitate?
Whose words are my menu and buttons in, mine or my customers'? Rewrite the labels.
Here are the problems from my last test. Which can I fix with the least change before the next round?

hire_for: Check the store against the ten usability rules and common site conventions, and test with five shoppers per round on real tasks.
store_questions: Check my store against the ten usability heuristics and list the worst problems first.
Does my store work the way shoppers expect from other sites they use? Where do I break conventions?
Rewrite my checkout error messages so they say what went wrong in plain words and how to fix it.
Plan three rounds of tests with five shoppers each, before and after my redesign.
Run the same tasks on two rival stores. What do they do better that I should borrow?
What is on my product page that shoppers rarely need?

hire_for: Design calm, restrained packaging and product lines that leave room for the buyer, and see the ordinary things you've stopped noticing.
store_questions: Is my packaging simple, or empty in a way that makes room for the buyer? What can I take away?
Will buyers feel a calm 'this will do', or a quick hunger that fades? Which should my brand aim for?
What ordinary thing about my product have I stopped seeing, and how could I redesign it?
What one material or mark could carry my whole brand idea across the range?
What hidden strength does my craft or region already have that my brand doesn't use?

hire_for: Find where and why the store leaks sales with research first, test messages with real buyers and respect sample size in A/B tests.
store_questions: My product page isn't converting. Plan the research in order: where the problems are, what they are, and why.
Can a stranger say what my landing page is about in five seconds? Score it on clarity, relevance, value and difference.
Does my ad's promise match the page it lands on? Plan the ad, traffic source and page together.
My A/B test looks like a winner after three days. Is the sample big enough, and has it run long enough?
Sort my list of store problems into buckets: fix tracking, investigate, test, or just do it.
What doubts is my checkout leaving unanswered, and how do I ask buyers what they think?

hire_for: Judge or brief a logo that identifies the store simply and distinctly, will last twenty years and doesn't try to explain everything.
store_questions: Does my logo identify my store, or try to explain what I sell? Run it through his seven tests.
Is my logo simple and distinct from every rival in my category? Could it be simpler?
Should I redesign my logo, or have people just not lived with it long enough yet?
What is the one idea behind my brand, and what symbol could carry it?
Set the rules for my ad layouts, then show me where the play is inside them.

hire_for: Turn store numbers into a clear chart and a one-line message that says what to notice and do next, without overclaiming.
store_questions: Turn my weekly sales spreadsheet into one chart and a message my business partner can act on.
Who will read my monthly report, and what question should each chart help them answer?
Write a title and a note for this chart that say what to notice first, without a cause I can't prove.
Remove the clutter from my dashboard but keep the details I need to check.
Are the periods and categories in my sales report comparable, like this month against a holiday month?
Compare two ways to show channel results to my client and pick the clearer one.

hire_for: Check product-market fit with the 'very disappointed' survey, fix first use before buying more ads, and rank tests by ICE score.
store_questions: Write the survey: how would my customers feel if they could no longer buy this? Do I pass 40 percent very disappointed?
Study my very disappointed customers: who are they, and what do they say the product does for them?
Should I buy more ads now, or fix product fit and first use first?
What is the one moment a customer gets the value from my product, and where do new buyers drop off before it?
Score my growth ideas on impact, confidence and ease from 1 to 10, and pick the top three to test this week.
Pick a North Star number for my store that grows over time and tracks with revenue.

hire_for: Find the real bottleneck, break blended acquisition cost apart by channel and plan for every ad channel to decay.
store_questions: Is my bottleneck repeat buying, first-time conversion or getting traffic? Draw my funnel in real numbers.
Break my blended cost per customer apart by channel. Which one is really expensive?
My best ad channel is getting worse. What happens when rivals copy it, and what is my next channel?
How many first-time buyers are still buying after 90 days, and what does that say about my product?
How could I build sharing into the product itself, so growth doesn't depend only on ads?
Will one more product or feature fix my sales, or is that the next feature fallacy?

hire_for: Research where your buyers really spend attention, show up there in proportion, and make content that helps without a click.
store_questions: Where do my buyers spend their attention: which podcasts, sites, creators and groups do they use more than most people?
Did I research my channels, or assume them? Pick the one or two that fit my buyers best.
If nobody clicks through to my store, does my post or answer still help and persuade? Rewrite it so it does.
How will I see the lift from my content beyond last clicks: brand searches, mentions or conversion rate?
Which business goal does my content plan tie to? Cut what doesn't connect.
Are people talking about my product's problem yet, before they search for it? Where can I play early?

hire_for: Plan store content from what buyers ask in their own words, beat the top result, promote every piece and track the emails it brings.
store_questions: What are my buyers searching for, in their own words, and which questions should my blog answer first?
Is my buying guide the most detailed, useful answer out there? Show me how to beat the top result.
Plan a weekly content calendar I can keep up for six months.
Who should I ask to share my new guide, and how would I word each note?
How many emails did my last guide bring in, and what is a subscriber worth to me?
Which numbers in my analytics are vanity numbers I should ignore?

hire_for: Post content made for each platform, give value several times before asking for the sale, and answer every comment like a shop visitor.
store_questions: Where is my customer's attention right now, and where is it cheaper than what I pay for ads?
Plan a week of posts made for each platform, not one video copied everywhere.
What have I given my followers before asking them to buy? Plan four value posts for each sales post.
How should I reply to comments and messages so each one feels like a customer walking into my shop?
I've been planning for months and posting nothing. What do I make today?
Do I really believe in this product? If not, what should I fix before I market it?

hire_for: Package product videos so people click and keep watching: title and thumbnail first, a first minute that pays off, then fix one thing.
store_questions: Would I click on this product video? Write the title and describe the thumbnail before we shoot.
Keep my title under about 50 characters and check the video really delivers its promise.
Does the first minute of my video deliver what the thumbnail promised?
Here is where viewers left my last video. What's the one thing to fix on the next one?
What's the wow moment a viewer can see in my product video, and can they see where the money went?
Which parts of my video shoot are critical, so that if one fails the whole video fails?

hire_for: Cut waste from order to cash: go and look, make only what the next step pulls, stop and fix defects at once, and ask why five times.
store_questions: Trace the time from a customer's order to cash in my hand. Where does the time go, and what can I cut?
Why is this stock sitting in my warehouse? Who asked for it? Set up reorders so I make or buy only what sells.
Orders keep shipping late. Ask why five times with me until we reach the real cause.
When a packing mistake happens, how do I stop the line at once so it can't reach more customers?
Write the standard way to pick and pack an order, timed by the best run, and tell me when to change it.
Which parts or steps should I do myself, and which should I buy in?

hire_for: Prepare hard talks with suppliers, stockists and angry customers: label their fears, ask calm how and what questions, skip the easy split.
store_questions: My supplier wants a 15 percent price rise. What are they afraid of losing, and how do I open the talk?
Write an accusation audit for my email telling a stockist our launch is late.
Give me three calibrated 'how' and 'what' questions for my factory call, so they solve my problem with me.
A buyer said yes too fast. How do I check it's a real yes and not a yes to end the call?
An angry customer wants a full refund and a public apology. Script my first two replies using labels.
Am I about to split the difference just to end the discomfort? What might I be missing?

hire_for: Negotiate with suppliers and partners on interests, not positions: know your walk-away option, invent packages and agree fair standards.
store_questions: My supplier insists on a 1,000-unit minimum. What interest sits under that demand, and what else could meet it?
If this supplier deal falls through, what can I really do next, and what will it cost? Check my fallback.
Invent four packages for my wholesale deal, mixing price, volume, payment terms and exclusivity, before we pick one.
What independent standard could justify a fair price to both of us, like published freight rates or market prices?
We agreed in principle. Write the commitment: who signs, what happens next and how we handle the first problem.

hire_for: Value your store, or one you might buy, by tying a three-sentence story to a few inputs, then give a range, not one number.
store_questions: Value my store: give me the story in three sentences, then the few numbers that follow from it.
I'm buying a small store at four times profit. Am I valuing it or pricing it, and what story does that price assume?
How much of my store's profit depends on me, the owner, and what does that do to its value?
What must my store spend to grow, and does that spending earn more than it costs?
Give me low, middle and high cases for my store's value and the two inputs that matter most.
What hurdle rate should a new product line clear before I put money into it?

hire_for: Size up your niche with the five forces, pick a clear position, decide what you will not do and make your activities fit together.
store_questions: Is this niche worth entering? Which of the five forces sets profits here: rivals, buyers, suppliers, new entrants or substitutes?
What is my position in one sentence: lower cost, a premium, or a narrow group served very well?
What am I choosing not to do? List what my store should give up.
Is my difference real, or am I just doing the same things a little better than rivals?
Map my value chain from design to delivery. Do my activities fit together so a rival can't copy them one at a time?
Does this new product line deepen my position or blur it?

hire_for: Find the job buyers hire your product to do, in what moment, and what they fire to hire you, then design around that.
store_questions: What job is my customer hiring my product to do, and in what moment? Write it with the practical, social and emotional sides.
Write the interview that walks recent buyers back through the day they decided to buy.
What did my customers fire, stop doing or stop buying to hire my product?
Who isn't buying in my category at all, and what do they do instead?
Where are people building their own workaround for this problem? Show me where to look.
Did customers use the product again after they bought it? How do I measure whether the job got done?

hire_for: Invert big store decisions: list what would surely make them fail, follow everyone's incentives and know where your knowledge ends.
store_questions: What would make my new product launch fail for sure? Am I doing any of it?
Who gets paid if I say yes to this agency, app or supplier, and how does that bend what they tell me?
Design a bonus plan for my team or affiliates. What will people do in response, and what does that cause?
Is this decision inside my circle of knowledge, or should it go in the too-hard basket?
What does my target need in plain numbers: how many buyers, at what price, out of how many?
State the case against my plan better than its critics would.

hire_for: Run wholesale and big-account sales calls with SPIN questions, so buyers state the cost of their problem and the value of your fix.
store_questions: Write my discovery call with a stockist: which situation questions can I skip by doing my homework first?
What problem questions will find what isn't working in a buyer's current range or supplier?
Give me implication questions that show what their problem costs them and who else it affects.
Write need-payoff questions so the buyer states the value of stocking my product in their own words.
Am I telling or asking on my sales calls? Review this call transcript.
How big is this corporate gifting sale, and how many meetings should I expect it to take?

hire_for: Decide whether to keep or quit a product, channel or launch by its future, not its sunk cost, with stop rules set in advance.
store_questions: Should I keep this slow product line or quit it? Fill the table: already spent, still owed, what changes next month.
My last launch flopped. Was it a bad decision or bad luck? Review what I knew before the result.
Set stop rules for my new ad channel: a review date and the numbers that would make me quit.
Which assumption in my plan most needs testing, and what small test would settle it?
What would I do with the money and time if I stopped this project?

hire_for: Cut customer effort in support and help stuck buyers decide: one clear recommendation, fewer options and the risk taken off.
store_questions: Where are my customers working too hard: tracking orders, returns or getting an answer?
Shoppers in chat can't decide between three products. Give me a reply that offers a personal pick and limits the options.
Is this buyer stuck because they doubt my product, or because they fear choosing wrong? How do I answer each?
What can I take off the table so the first order feels safe: a trial, an easy swap or a guarantee?
Should my product page say what not to buy, even from my own range, when a cheaper option fits?
What do my best support agents do that the average ones don't? Review these tickets.

hire_for: Get the truth from customer conversations: ask what people last did and spent, not whether they like your idea.
store_questions: Rewrite my customer interview questions so they ask what people last did, not 'would you buy this?'
What am I trying to learn from these chats, in one sentence? Help me write it before I talk to anyone.
Narrow who I should talk to until I can name a person and a place to find them.
Sort my interview notes: set compliments aside, pin fluff to real moments and trace each feature request to its reason.
Which scary question am I avoiding about my product idea?
Did anyone give up something real, like time, an introduction or a pre-order, or only say nice things?

hire_for: Turn product use into a habit buyers keep, so they reorder: a tiny first step, an anchor in their day and a quick feeling of success.
store_questions: Buyers of my skincare stop using it after two weeks. At the moment they skip it, what makes it hard to do?
What is the smallest version of using my product that a buyer could manage even on a tired day?
What do my buyers already do reliably that using my product could follow, like making morning coffee?
Write my post-purchase emails as a habit recipe: the anchor, the tiny step and a small celebration.
My buyers' routine slipped after the holidays. Did the habit fail or did their situation change, and how do I help them restart?

hire_for: Write newsletters and pages to one real reader, put their biggest worry first and cut every sentence any brand could send.
store_questions: Who is the one person reading my store newsletter? Describe them before I write a word.
What worry sits under the search that brings people to my buying guide, and is the answer at the top?
Could this sentence appear in any store's email? Rewrite it the way only I would say it.
Open my next newsletter with a moment I noticed, not a topic.
How will my readers write back, and how should I answer the replies?

hire_for: Write to one hungry buyer using what your support team hears, pass the 'would I bet the business on this' test, then plan the second offer.
store_questions: Who's the one person reading my product page, and what are they already hunting for?
What do my support team and packers hear customers ask about? Turn it into selling points I've missed.
Would I send this email if my whole business hung on it? Mark every line that wouldn't pass.
What's the cheapest way to find out by Friday whether this offer works, using my own list or a small ad spend?
What's the second offer, right after someone buys?
Which parts of my week bring in money, and which just eat time I could hand off?

hire_for: Win repeat orders and referrals: thank every buyer the same day, keep a customer file and treat each complaint as the next sale.
store_questions: What do I do for customers after they buy? Plan what happens in the first week after an order.
Write a same-day thank-you note for new buyers that feels personal, not like a receipt.
What should my customer file record after each sale, so later messages talk about what matters to them?
Here is my complaint pile. How do I move first on each one and turn it into the next sale?
Why would a buyer come back to me instead of the cheaper store down the road?
How do I ask happy customers for referrals without being pushy?

hire_for: Make a known product feel fresh with a small edit, a word on the label or a collab, then ship the first version fast.
store_questions: What does everyone already know and love in my category, and what's the smallest change that makes it new?
Does my next drop speak to both the newcomer and the long-time fan?
What word or label could I add to my product or pack that makes people look again?
Which brand, artist or creator outside my field would make a good collab, and what would each side bring?
This design has sat on my laptop for months. What can I put out this week?
Who is left out of my brand, and how do I go and ask how they actually use products like mine?

hire_for: Find who can't use your store and why, from small screens to screen readers and slow connections, and fix the mismatch for everyone.
store_questions: Who tries to buy from my store and can't? List what my checkout demands of eyes, hands, language, time and connection.
What changes for a shopper on my store in a noisy, slow or unfamiliar setting, like a phone on a train?
What workaround are customers already using, like emailing their order, that shows a gap in my store?
Whose expertise is missing from my store design, and how do I bring those shoppers in early?
Does my other route, like phone ordering, give the same status and convenience as the main one?
Which habit in my theme or templates keeps creating this problem, and what check stops it?

hire_for: Turn a flat brief into one big idea, a striking image fused with a short line, that people pass on for free.
store_questions: What's the big idea for my launch? Say it in one sentence.
Can a shopper get my ad in one look while scrolling fast? Do the picture and the line make one point?
Will people pass my ad on for free? What would make the press or strangers share it?
Give me a thumbnail or cover idea for my product: one striking image and a short line.
Test panels disliked my bold idea. Is it bad, or just unfamiliar?

hire_for: Grow through creators, meet-ups and customer talk the way Gymshark did, before you buy reach or sell through other shops.
store_questions: Which ten creators should I send my product to first, and what should I ask them for?
How do I run a meet-up or pop-up that builds regulars, not just a one-day sales spike?
My customers keep asking for things I don't sell. How do I turn that into my next product?
A big retailer wants to stock us. Should I say yes or keep selling only on my own site?
I'm doing everything in the business. What should I hand over first, and to whom?

hire_for: Turn reviews, comments and content into products and a voice buyers share, the way Glossier grew mostly by word of mouth.
store_questions: I have hundreds of reviews and comments. How do I turn them into a brief for my next product?
How do I ask customers to help shape a product without letting a vote make the call?
My captions and emails sound like ads. How do I make them sound like a text to a friend?
How do I turn my most loyal buyers into a referral or ambassador group?
What should I publish so people follow my store even when they're not buying?

hire_for: Remove the one fear that stops people buying your product online, with a try-at-home, sample or return offer you can afford, like Warby Parker.
store_questions: People say they need to try my product before buying. What risk-free offer can I afford?
What frustrates buyers most in my category, and how do I make that my headline offer?
Can I price lower by selling direct, and will my margins hold up?
My launch might sell out. What do I set up before it goes live?
Should I open a showroom or pop-up, and how do I pick the city?

hire_for: Say your offer in one funny, true line and launch it with a low-cost video, the way Dollar Shave Club did, with a plan for if it works.
store_questions: Can you write a short, funny launch video script for my product that I can shoot myself?
How do I say my offer in one line that beats buying it in a shop?
My brand sounds like everyone else. How do I make it plain, bold and a bit funny?
If my video takes off, what will break first and how do I get ready?
My members buy one thing every month. What should I add next, and in what order?

hire_for: Raise order value and repeat sales: pre-sell content, one-click offers after checkout, email and text, launch build-up, like BOOM.
store_questions: What should I offer buyers the moment after they pay, and at what price?
Only a small share of my revenue is from repeat buyers. What do I fix first?
Should my ads go to a product page or to a helpful article first?
How many emails a week should I send, and who should get texts instead?
Can I raise my prices, and which ones should I test before I change them?
How do I build up a new product launch so it sells on day one?
